title: How Real Estate Agents Get Recommended by ChatGPT and Google AI
seoTitle: How Agents Get Recommended by ChatGPT and Google AI
seoDescription: Where ChatGPT and Google AI get information about real estate agents, what makes them name you, what does not help, and how to check what they say today.
excerpt: AI tools can only vouch for what they can find in public, so the agents they name are the ones with clear, consistent pages, profiles and reviews.
imageAlt: Two people relaxing on a sofa in a living room, each looking at a smartphone
imageIdea: Real photo of people at home researching on their phones, daylight, screens not visible, lived in room, no staged stock look.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Real estate agents get recommended by ChatGPT and Google AI when those tools can find clear, consistent, public information that ties your name to a place and a type of client. That means indexed web pages about who you help and where, a complete Google Business Profile with real reviews, and the same facts everywhere else your name appears. No one controls the answer, but you can make yourself easy to find, check and cite.

This question usually comes up after an agent types "best realtor in" plus their town into ChatGPT and sees a competitor's name. Here is what I can say with confidence, and where the honest answer is "nobody knows yet."

Do buyers and sellers really ask AI to pick an agent?

Some do, but I have not found a reliable public count of how many, so I will not quote one. What is well documented is that agents still sit at the center of the transaction, which is why the question of who gets named matters.

In the National Association of Realtors 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers, 88% of buyers purchased through an agent or broker. NAR's release on the same report says 91% of buyers would use their agent again or recommend them. A recommendation from a friend and a recommendation from an AI tool work the same way: someone vouches for you before you ever talk. The difference is that the AI tool can only vouch for what it can find in public.

Where do ChatGPT and Google AI get information about agents?

Google's AI features link to pages from its normal search index, and ChatGPT search pulls from third party search providers and partner content. Neither one reads your CRM or your closed deals. They read what is public.

ToolWhat its own documentation saysWhat you control
Google AI Overviews and AI ModeA page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet in Search to appear as a supporting link, with no extra technical requirements (Google).Your website pages, and your Google Business Profile.
ChatGPT searchUses third party search providers and content from partners (OpenAI), and may share an approximate location with trusted providers to show nearby business listings (OpenAI Help).Your website, and the listings and profiles those providers pick up.
ChatGPT and your websiteSites that block OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers, though they can still appear as navigational links (OpenAI).Your robots.txt file and any firewall or bot blocking your web host applies.

OpenAI does not name which provider supplies local business listings, so I am not going to guess. The practical lesson holds either way: if your information is thin or inconsistent across the places a search provider looks, an AI answer has little to work with.

What makes an AI tool comfortable naming you?

Specific, consistent, verifiable information. A tool answering "who is a good listing agent for condos in Old Town Scottsdale" needs to find pages and profiles that say you do exactly that, plus signals from clients that back it up.

  • A page for each thing you are known for. If you work with first time buyers in Mesa or sell horse property in Queen Creek, say so on its own page, with real detail a client would want: price ranges you work in, how you handle inspections, what the area is like. Vague "serving the Valley" copy gives an AI tool nothing to match.
  • A complete Google Business Profile. Correct category, service area, hours, website link and photos. Google says complete and accurate information makes a business easier to match with the right searches.
  • Reviews that describe the work. A review that says, for example, "she sold our townhouse in nine days and handled the HOA paperwork" tells a reader, and any tool summarizing reviews, much more than "great agent."
  • The same facts everywhere. Your name, brokerage, phone and areas should match across your website, your brokerage roster page, your profile and the portals you already use. Conflicting details make you harder to confirm.
  • A website search tools can read. Check that your robots.txt does not block Google or OAI-SearchBot, and that your key pages are not hidden inside an IDX widget or a PDF.

What does not help?

Shortcuts. Google says llms.txt files and similar AI specific markup are not needed for its search features. Fifty near identical neighborhood pages with the town name swapped also fall under Google's spam policies, which describe doorway abuse and scaled content abuse. Write fewer pages that each say something true and useful.

How can you check what AI says about you today?

Ask it the way a client would, write down what you see, and repeat it monthly. Use five to ten prompts, such as "best real estate agent for first time buyers in Gilbert" and "who should I talk to about selling a home in Ahwatukee," plus one that asks what the tool knows about you by name.

Treat each answer as a snapshot. Results vary by location, wording and the person asking. To see actual visits, OpenAI says ChatGPT adds utm_source=chatgpt.com to links it sends, so those visits show up in your website analytics. Google says traffic from AI Overviews and AI Mode is counted in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type.

Where does social media fit?

Social keeps your name familiar to the people who already know you, and that is where most referrals and reviews start. I have not seen documentation showing that AI tools cite agent social posts when they recommend someone, so I would not sell it that way. What it does is keep a steady stream of past clients thinking of you, which feeds the reviews and referrals above.

Consistency is the hard part for busy agents. That is why we built LocalLift Signature, a done for you weekly posting service for agents and title reps. For search, profile and AI visibility work, see our real estate marketing page.

Questions we hear

Can I pay to be recommended by ChatGPT or Google AI?

Not in the organic answers. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode link to pages that are indexed and eligible for a snippet, and OpenAI says ChatGPT search draws on third party search providers and partner content. Be wary of anyone who sells a guaranteed AI placement.

Do I need an llms.txt file on my website?

Not for Google. Google says llms.txt files and similar AI specific markup are not needed and do not affect visibility in its Search features. Spend that time on clear pages about who you help and where.

Does my Google Business Profile matter for AI answers?

It is one of the most visible public records of your business, with your category, service area and reviews in one place. Google has not published how much its AI features lean on it for agent searches, so I treat it as necessary, not sufficient.

How often should I check what AI tools say about me?

Monthly is enough for most agents. Use the same prompts each time, write down who gets named, and treat any single answer as a snapshot, since results change with location and wording.

Will posting on social media get me into AI answers?

I have not seen documentation showing that ChatGPT or Google AI cite agent social posts for recommendations. Social earns its place by keeping you familiar to your sphere, which is where referrals and reviews come from.

takeaways: ChatGPT and Google AI can only recommend an agent based on information they can find in public.
Google says a page must be indexed and eligible for a snippet to appear as a link in AI Overviews and AI Mode.
Specific pages, a complete Google Business Profile, detailed reviews and consistent facts make an agent easier to name.
Check what AI tools say about you monthly with the same prompts, and treat each answer as a snapshot.
